newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav wheat imports seen at 300-400,000 tonnes.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav wheat imports seen at 300-400,000 tonnes.

text.p: Yugoslavia, facing an acute grain shortage after its worst harvest in 25 years and excessive exports in 1995/96, is in the process of importing 300,000-400,000 tonnes of wheat.
Producers said the government ignored analysts who warned against wheat exports last year because of a lack of stocks to feed a population swollen by the number of war refugees.

"We warned the government on inevitable shortage of wheat even before last year's harvest," said Ljiljana Vasic, president of the association of agricultural cooperatives from the wheat-region of Vojvodina.
"They now must import to provide at least bread to an already impoverished population," she said.
Government officials concede in private that official stocks are lower than has been admitted in public and inadequate to meet estimated annual needs of 2.5 million tonnes.
Vukosav Sakovic, head of the Yugoslav grains fund, told Reuters that the federal trade ministry late last year set a quota of 300,000 tonnes for wheat imports in 1996.

"We estimate that about 20,000 tonnes reached the country by the end of December last year", he said, adding that many barges loaded with wheat for Yugoslavia were delayed due to bad weather and ice on the Danube.
"But we expect that about 100,000 tonnes will reach our ports by the end of January," Savkovic said.
Some analysts said Yugoslavia exported about 380,000 tonnes of the 1995 wheat crop, but now it would have to pay twice the price to import the same quantity.
Officials declined to disclose 1997 wheat import plans, but a source close to the government said the import quota was set at 400,000 tonnes and exports limited to 500,000.
Sakovic said the fund estimated a wheat shortage of 500,000 tonnes, but added that it was very difficult if not impossible to obtain accurate data on government stocks.
Vasic said limited transport capacity meant that the imported wheat might arrive at the time as the local harvest. "Then it would have an adverse effect on our own production."

Agriculture ministry spokesman Milan Prostran said it took 10 months for former Yugoslavia to export two million tonnes of wheat. "Serbia always had a wheat surplus. We endured even four years of war and sanctions without wheat imports."
Yugoslavia reduced its wheat area in 1995 by 300,000 hectares to 582,965 ha.
According to the government statistics office, the 1996 wheat harvest dropped to a 25-year low of 1.5 million tonnes, down from 2.97 million the previous year.
Yields were at their lowest since 1972, falling to 2.96 tonnes per hectare from 3.4 tonnes the previous year. -- Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom ++381 11 222 4254
